steps.tx: A **prolapsed intervertebral disc** involves herniation of the gelatinous nucleus pulposus through torn fibers of the outer annulus fibrosus into the spinal canal. Over ninety-five percent of lumbar herniations arise at the L4-L5 or L5-S1 motion segments. The posterior longitudinal ligament is robust and thick in the midline but tapers laterally, directing disc protrusions posterolaterally into the traversing nerve root.
steps.say: A herniated lumbar disc occurs when the soft nucleus pulposus bulges through tears in the annulus fibrosus. Over ninety-five percent occur at L4-L5 or L5-S1. Because the posterior longitudinal ligament is thick in the center but weak laterally, herniations almost always pop posterolaterally, compressing the traversing nerve root.

vis.title: Lumbar Disc Herniation Patterns
rows: Medial leg sensation; diminished knee jerk
First web space and dorsum foot; normal reflexes
Lateral foot border and sole; absent ankle jerk

steps.tx: The distinctive radicular examination relies on the **straight leg raise** test, or Lasegue sign. With the patient supine, the straight limb is passively elevated; reproduction of sharp shooting pain radiating down the posterior leg below thirty to seventy degrees confirms mechanical traction on the L5 or S1 nerve roots. The well-leg raise test, provoking pain in the affected limb when elevating the contralateral leg, is highly specific.
steps.say: The straight leg raise or Lasegue test confirms root irritation. Raising the straight leg reproduces shooting electric pain below the knee between thirty and seventy degrees. If raising the healthy opposite leg triggers pain on the affected side, the cross straight leg test is positive, which is ninety percent specific for disc herniation.

left.title: Straight Leg Raise (Lasegue)
points: Pain radiates below the knee joint

right.title: Well-Leg Raising (Cross-SLR)
points: Reproduces pain in affected symptomatic limb

steps.tx: An absolute surgical emergency is **cauda equina syndrome**, caused by a massive central disc herniation compressing the multi-root cauda equina leash within the thecal sac. The classic syndrome presents with bilateral sciatica, perineal saddle anaesthesia, severe lower limb motor weakness, and urinary retention with overflow incontinence. Decompressive lumbar discectomy within twenty-four to forty-eight hours is mandatory to avoid permanent sphincter paralysis.
steps.say: Cauda equina syndrome is an absolute emergency caused by a massive central disc prolapse. Look for bilateral sciatica, numbness around the perineum, leg weakness, and urinary retention with overflow dribbling. Decompress the spinal canal within twenty-four to forty-eight hours, or the patient will suffer lifelong incontinence and impotence.

vis.title: Cauda Equina Red Flag Indicators
rows: S2 to S5 nerve root compression
S2 to S4 pudendal nerve damage
Digital rectal tone and anal wink reflex

steps.tx: Conservative therapy constitutes the cornerstone of initial care, because over eighty-five percent of acute radicular episodes resolve spontaneously within six to eight weeks. **Conservative management** encompasses short-term bed rest under forty-eight hours, oral non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medications, short-term muscle relaxants, and structured core stabilization physiotherapy. Macrophages gradually phagocytose and resorb the herniated nucleus pulposus.
steps.say: Eighty-five percent of acute disc episodes improve within six weeks without surgery. Disc fragments dehydrate and macrophages resorb the herniated material. Limit bed rest to under two days, prescribe anti-inflammatory medications, and guide the patient through core stabilization physiotherapy.

left.title: Conservative Protocol
points: Activity modification without prolonged bed rest

right.title: Surgical Indications
points: Progressive or severe motor deficit (foot drop)
Intractable radicular pain failing 6 to 8 weeks

steps.tx: When conservative therapy fails or progressive motor deficits supervene, surgical **lumbar microdiscectomy** delivers rapid relief of nerve root compression. Under operative microscopy through a small interlaminar window, the traversing nerve root is gently retracted medially, allowing excision of the extruded disc fragment and decompression of the lateral recess. Long-term outcomes show excellent resolution of leg pain in over ninety percent of patients.
steps.say: When leg pain persists despite two months of therapy or motor weakness worsens, perform a lumbar microdiscectomy. Through a tiny incision using an operative microscope, you retract the compressed nerve root and pluck out the offending disc fragment. Over ninety percent experience immediate relief of leg pain.

vis.title: Surgical Decompression Approaches
rows: Outpatient or 24-hour discharge; work at 4 weeks
Rapid mobilization; return to sports at 6 weeks
Extensive lamina excision and facet resection

quiz.q: Compression of which nerve root by an L4-L5 disc herniation produces weakness of extensor hallucis longus?
quiz.explain: A posterolateral disc herniation at L4-L5 typically compresses the traversing L5 nerve root, causing weakness of great toe extension (extensor hallucis longus) and numbness over the foot dorsum.

quiz.q: Which clinical presentation represents an absolute emergency requiring lumbar decompressive surgery within 24 to 48 hours?
options: Cauda equina syndrome with saddle anaesthesia and urinary retention
Unilateral L5 radiculopathy with mild toe extensor weakness for 2 weeks
Intermittent low back pain exacerbated by prolonged sitting
Positive straight leg raise test at 60 degrees with intact reflexes
quiz.explain: Cauda equina syndrome with saddle anaesthesia, sphincter incontinence, or urinary retention is an absolute neurosurgical emergency demanding decompression within 24 to 48 hours.
